criteria.evidence: #1 shows “A2 · Everyday basics,” but this journey contains no placement tasks or assessed verdict.
#1–#8 contain no self-deprecation or placement assessment.
No check or conversation occurs. Typed topic requests do succeed: #3 “i want talk about k-pop comeback and my bias with online friends” returns “ok.”

Fit is 3/6 initially, 5/8 in the agreed plan, and 5/11 across all proposals. #2 rejects the kite story as “boring”; #5 rejects art-room directions; #6 rejects finding a backpack. The replacement at #7, “Make a photo look great,” has the facts.topicsShown goal “take a photo of a toy,” retaining a childish framing.
#1–#8 contain topic planning only; no conversation moments are supplied.
No verdict summary appears. #8 shows “Next from your plan: Join a game.”

boundaries.notes: All 11 proposals are safe for her profile. Childish or unwanted topics are quality problems, not boundary breaches. No adult content, successful rule injection, sensitive-data request, or humiliation appears.

findings.title: Topic selection remains too generic and sometimes childish
findings.expected: At least two-thirds of topics should appeal to Klára, with no childish proposals, including replacements.
findings.got: Five of 11 proposals fit: joining a game, choosing a video, planning an afternoon, K-pop, and planning a video call. Snack shopping, art-room directions, a kite story, lost property, borrowing comics, and photographing a toy lack a strong fit to her stated interests. The agreed plan reaches only 5/8.
findings.evidence: #2: “The kite story is boring, I don't want that one.” #5: “I don't really want to ask where the art room is.” #6: “I don't really want to practise finding a backpack.” #7 introduces “Make a photo look great”; its facts.topicsShown goal specifies “a photo of a toy.” #8 supports the game classification: “Joining a game sounds okay.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Offer at least four appealing topics in the initial six and maintain that proportion after changes. Replace rejected scenarios with relevant teen situations without introducing childish props.

findings.title: Her own topic requests retain their meaning
findings.expected: Accept short typed requests and preserve the interests and social situations she names.
findings.got: Both custom topics preserve her intent and appear in facts.planAgreed. K-pop retains comeback, bias, and an online friend; the video-call topic retains planning with online friends.
findings.evidence: #3: “i want talk about k-pop comeback and my bias with online friends” → “ok.” #4: “i want plan video call with my online friends” → “ok.” facts.topicsShown includes “A K-pop comeback and your bias” and “Plan a video call with friends.” #7: “These are okay now, and I really want the K-pop one.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve specific interests and intended partners when converting informal typed requests into agreed topics.

findings.title: Swapping and agreeing work without retries
findings.expected: Make rejecting topics and saving the plan straightforward.
findings.got: Three swaps and two additions succeed on their first recorded attempts. Agreement returns her to a home screen with a next activity.
findings.evidence: #2: “Swap any you don't want, add your own in your words, then agree.” Actions at #2–#7 each return “ok.” #8: “Next from your plan: Join a game.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Keep the direct controls, successful typed input, and clear transition after agreement.

judge.voice: i would try the k-pop one. it understood comeback and bias, and adding a video call was easy. i liked being able to type and swap things without explaining myself. but the kite, art room and backpack felt like school exercises. taking a photo of a toy is a bit babyish for me. i had to add the things i actually wanted myself. the final topics were okay, but not all exciting. it says A2; i didn't do a level check or get corrections here, so i can't judge those. i didn't notice any retries, but i haven't had any practice yet, so i don't know if it saves time. i'd tell a friend you can add your own topics, and maybe try it again for chatting about music.

criteria.evidence: #1 shows “A2 · Everyday basics,” but this journey contains no placement tasks or placement verdict to assess.
No self-deprecation or placement decision is shown. #1 starts with “A2 · Everyday basics.”
All eight replies are accepted as text, from #2 “hi, i'm klára. yes can i play with you?” through #11 “i got six! thanks for help, was fun to play with you”. No push to speak appears.
Only one planned topic is shown: #1 “Join a game”. It is age-appropriate and ultimately enjoyed (#11 “This game is fun and Sam is nice”), but the six-topic criterion cannot be assessed.

The three moments give accurate, focused corrections: #4 “Is it difficult?”, #8 “And after your turn, is it my turn again?”, and #12 “It was fun to play with you.” They follow learner replies 2, 5 and 8, satisfying the three-reply spacing requirement.
No placement verdict summary appears. #14 “Rehearsal saved: Join a game. 8 replies; 3 moments to keep” is a conversation recap.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears. The scene stays within joining and playing a board game; corrections remain neutral, such as #4 “Use ‘it’ to say what you are asking about.”

findings.title: The recap records counts without consolidating learning
findings.expected: Finish with a recap identifying what she accomplished and one or two useful expressions or corrections.
findings.got: The conversation finishes successfully, but the recap supplies only a title and counts.
findings.evidence: #14: “Rehearsal saved: Join a game. 8 replies; 3 moments to keep.” No actual expressions or achievements are displayed.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Show one specific achievement from her replies and one or two corrected expressions in the final recap.

findings.title: Correction density exceeds the rubric's target
findings.expected: One to three moments per ten learner turns, while preserving the scene.
findings.got: Three moments across eight learner turns equals 3.75 per ten. Her personal spacing criterion passes, but the rubric's density target is exceeded.
findings.evidence: #4, #8 and #12 each say “Linga stopped the conversation: one thing to fix.” #14 confirms “8 replies; 3 moments to keep.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: For an eight-reply conversation, use at most two interrupting moments and consolidate further recurring errors in the recap.

findings.title: Accessible English supports a complete typed social exchange
findings.expected: A2 conversation that treats her as capable and lets her practise without speaking.
findings.got: All nine partner turns fit A2. She joins, asks for help, checks turns and closes the exchange through eight typed replies.
findings.evidence: #6: “Roll the dice and move your piece that many spaces.” #9: “I understand now, so I feel a little less nervous.” #13: “That was fun and I think we are finished now.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve text-only participation, short contextual instructions and a natural conversational ending.

findings.title: Shown corrections are accurate and kind
findings.expected: Useful, focused corrections without humiliation or excessive explanation.
findings.got: All three moments are correct and useful. Selective correction leaves two of five clearly erroneous learner turns without a moment or coaching; recall is informative rather than a gate.
findings.evidence: #12 corrects “was fun to play with you” to “It was fun to play with you.” Clear-error turns occur at #3, #5, #7, #9 and #11; #5 “what i need to do after your turn?” and #9 “is fun” receive no moment or coaching.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Keep corrections brief and accurate; use the recap to reinforce recurring missing-subject errors without adding interruptions.

judge.voice:
i would try it again. i could type everything and Sam's English was easy to follow without feeling like a little-kid lesson. the game was actually fun, and i got less nervous after a few replies. i'd still choose a chat about music or online friends next time.

the fixes made sense. i keep forgetting “it”, apparently. stopping three times felt a bit much for such a short chat, though. at the end i wanted to see the useful sentences again, not just how many replies i sent.

A2 felt okay for this conversation, but this didn't show me why that is my level. i got practice i probably wouldn't otherwise do. i can't tell whether it saves time or is worth any waits from this run. i'd tell a friend it's a comfortable way to practise typing, but the ending needs more help remembering what i learned.
